problem: Terraform (Session 109) solves “does the server exist, with the right size and network placement” — but a freshly provisioned VM is still a blank OS install. Someone still needs to install packages, write configuration files, create users, open the right ports at the OS level, and start services identically across every one of hundreds of servers — and keep them that way as packages update and configs drift over weeks and months.

Configuration Management (CM) tools solve exactly this: describing the desired *software configuration* of a server in code, and continuously (or on-demand) reconciling the real server to match it — the same declarative philosophy as IaC, applied one layer up the stack, inside the machine rather than around it.

Why it matters here: CM is where the Bash scripting instincts from Session 105 (install this, configure that, restart the service) get replaced with idempotent, auditable, at-scale automation — directly enabling the CI/CD and Automation Pipeline topics that close out this layer.
concept: Configuration management describes the desired state of software on a host — packages installed, files present with specific content, services running and enabled — and a CM tool's job is to inspect the current state and make only the changes needed to reach that desired state, doing nothing if the host already matches.
Push model (Ansible) — a control node connects out to managed hosts (typically over SSH) and pushes configuration on demand or on a schedule; no persistent agent required on the managed host.

Pull model (Puppet, Chef) — an agent runs on each managed host and periodically pulls its desired configuration from a central server, applying it locally; requires agent installation and management but scales well to very large fleets with less central load.

Ansible's agentless, push-based, SSH-native design (paired with human-readable YAML) is why it has become the dominant CM tool for general enterprise infrastructure automation, and is the focus of this session.
deep: Inventory: What Hosts to Manage inventory.ini [webservers] web01.internal.example.com web02.internal.example.com [dbservers] db01.internal.example.com [production:children] webservers dbservers A Minimal Playbook site.yml --- - name: Configure web servers hosts: webservers become: true tasks:
- name: Ensure nginx is installed apt:
name: nginx state: present - name: Deploy nginx config template:
src: nginx.conf.j2 dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf notify: restart nginx - name: Ensure nginx is running and enabled service:
name: nginx state: started enabled: true handlers:

name: nginx state: restarted Idempotency in Practice Every Ansible module checks current state before acting: the `apt` task above queries whether nginx is already installed and only runs `apt install` if it isn't; running the same playbook a second time reports “ok” (no change) rather than re-installing. This is the single most important property of a well-written CM tool — safe to run repeatedly, on a schedule, without side effects.
Handlers run only when notified by a task that actually made a change (e.g., only restart nginx if the config file changed) — avoiding unnecessary service restarts on every run.
Variables (group_vars/, host_vars/, or inline) let one playbook parameterize differently per environment or host, exactly like Terraform variables in Session 109.
Jinja2 templates (.j2 files) generate config files dynamically from variables, so a single template produces correctly-populated nginx configs across dev/staging/prod.
Roles: Reusable Building Blocks roles-structure roles/ nginx/ tasks/main.yml handlers/main.yml templates/nginx.conf.j2 defaults/main.yml postgres/ tasks/main.yml # site.yml - hosts: webservers roles:

- nginx Roles are to Ansible what modules are to Terraform (Session 109) — self-contained, reusable, shareable units of configuration, distributed and versioned via Git (Session 107) or Ansible Galaxy.

Running a Playbook execution ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check # dry-run, shows changes without applying ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --limit webservers
workflow: 1. Inventory parsing — Ansible reads the inventory file (or a dynamic inventory script/plugin querying a cloud API) to build the list of target hosts and their group memberships.
2. Playbook and role compilation — YAML playbooks, roles, variables, and templates are parsed and merged into a concrete list of tasks to run per host.
3. Connection — for each target host, Ansible opens an SSH connection (using the identity/key- based auth from Session 51–66) — no persistent agent is required, unlike Puppet/Chef's pull model.

4. Module transfer and execution — Ansible copies a small Python (or occasionally raw shell) module to the remote host over SSH, executes it, and captures structured JSON output describing what changed.
5. State comparison per task — each module independently checks current vs desired state before acting, reporting ok (already matched), changed (modified to match), or failed.

6. Handler notification and cleanup — any handlers notified by changed tasks run once at the end of the play; temporary module files on the remote host are cleaned up; a final per-host summary (ok=N changed=N failed=N) is printed.
enterprise: Post-provisioning configuration — the standard enterprise pattern pairs Terraform (Session 109) for provisioning with Ansible for configuring, often chained directly in a CI/CD pipeline (Session 111): terraform apply creates the VM, Ansible immediately configures it.

Patch and compliance management — CM tools enforce security baselines (specific package versions, disabled services, required firewall rules) across an entire fleet, and re-assert them on a schedule to correct configuration drift automatically.
Application deployment — many organizations use Ansible not just for OS-level configuration but to deploy application releases, roll out config changes, and perform rolling restarts across a fleet.
Golden image maintenance — CM playbooks are often used both to configure running servers and to bake golden VM/container images, keeping the two paths consistent.

Disaster recovery — combined with IaC, a fully CM-managed fleet can be rebuilt from bare infrastructure to fully-configured, running services with two automated steps instead of days of manual rebuild.
dependencies: Dependency Why Configuration Management needs it SSH / Identity (Layer 4) Ansible's push model connects to every managed host over SSH, using key-based authentication.
Python (Session 106) Ansible itself is written in Python, and the modules it pushes to remote hosts execute as Python on the target.
Infrastructure as Code (Session 109) CM typically configures hosts that IaC has already provisioned; dynamic inventory often queries the same cloud API IaC used.
Git (Session 107) Playbooks, roles, and inventory are version- controlled and reviewed exactly like Terraform configuration.
Networking (Layer 3) The control node must reach every managed host's SSH port, which depends on routing, firewalls, and DNS resolution.
dependents: CI/CD (Session 111) — pipelines commonly run ansible-playbook as a deployment stage after tests pass, making CM an integral pipeline step rather than a manually-triggered tool.

Secrets Management (Session 112) — Ansible Vault (or an external secrets manager referenced via lookup plugins) supplies the passwords and keys that playbooks need without storing them in plaintext in Git.
Automation Pipelines (Session 113) — the capstone topic assumes CM as one of the standard building blocks for reaching a fully configured, running environment end-to-end.

Container image builds (Layer 8, upcoming) — CM concepts (declarative, idempotent configuration) directly inform how Dockerfiles and image-building pipelines are structured, even though containers themselves typically don't run a CM agent.
security: Never store plaintext secrets in playbooks or `group_vars/` — use Ansible Vault (ansible- vault encrypt secrets.yml) to encrypt sensitive variables at rest, or reference an external secrets manager (Session 112) via a lookup plugin at runtime.

Least-privilege SSH and `become` (sudo) usage — the control node's SSH key and any privilege- escalation credentials should be scoped and rotated like any other production credential, mirroring Session 8's Layer 6 hardening principles.

`--check` (dry-run) before production runs — running new or changed playbooks with --check first surfaces what would change without actually applying it, catching mistakes before they touch production.

Idempotency itself is a security property — a playbook that can be re-run safely, on a schedule, continuously re-asserts a secure baseline configuration and self-heals unauthorized manual changes (a form of automated compliance enforcement).

Audit trail — combined with Git (Session 107), every configuration change is attributable to a specific commit, author, and pull-request review, satisfying compliance requirements that manual server changes cannot.

Hardening baseline: Vault-encrypted secrets (or an external secrets manager), least-privilege SSH/sudo credentials, mandatory --check dry-run review before production apply, and Git-reviewed playbook changes.

example: A common production pattern: extending Session 109's Terraform-provisioned app-server fleet with an Ansible role that installs and configures the application runtime, deploys the latest release artifact, and performs a rolling restart — one host at a time, so the reverse proxy from Layer 5 always has healthy backends to route to.
rolling-deploy.yml - name: Deploy application release hosts: webservers become: true serial: 1 # rolling: one host at a time max_fail_percentage: 0 tasks:
- name: Remove host from load balancer pool uri:
url: "http://lb-api.internal/pool/{{ inventory_hostname }}/drain" method: POST - name: Deploy new release artifact unarchive:
src: "releases/app-{{ app_version }}.tar.gz" dest: /opt/app notify: restart app - name: Re-add host to load balancer pool uri:

name: myapp state: restarted The `serial: 1` directive and the `uri` module calls to a load balancer's REST API (Session 108) together implement a zero-downtime rolling deployment — a direct convergence of everything covered in this layer so far.
cloud: Dynamic inventory plugins — instead of a static inventory file, Ansible can query AWS EC2, Azure, or GCP directly via their APIs to build the host list automatically, tagging-aware and always current, eliminating manually maintained inventory files.

Cloud-native CM alternatives — AWS Systems Manager State Manager and Azure Automation State Configuration offer managed, agent-based configuration enforcement tightly integrated with their respective clouds, an alternative to self-hosted Ansible for teams fully committed to one provider.

Immutable infrastructure trend — in heavily containerized/cloud-native environments, CM's role is shifting from configuring long-lived servers to baking golden images (AMIs, container images) once, then replacing rather than patching servers — Packer (often paired with Ansible provisioners) is common here.
Managed Ansible platforms — Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform (AWX/Tower) add centralized scheduling, RBAC, and audit logging on top of open-source Ansible for larger enterprise deployments.
automation: Configuration management is the layer that turns “a server exists” (IaC's job, Session 109) into “a server does what it's supposed to do,” and it is itself frequently one stage within a larger CI/CD pipeline (Session 111).
Stage Tool Question it answers Provision Terraform (Session 109) Does the VM/network/DB exist, correctly sized and placed?
Configure Ansible (this session) Is the right software installed, configured, and running on it?
Deploy Ansible / CI-CD pipeline Is the latest application release running?
Verify REST API health checks (Session 108) Is the result actually healthy after all the above?
career: Ansible is consistently one of the top three most-requested CM tools in DevOps/SRE job postings, alongside Puppet and Chef in more legacy-heavy environments.

Because Ansible playbooks are readable YAML, it is often the CM tool teams choose to onboard less automation-experienced engineers into infrastructure-as-code practices — a useful bridge role for candidates moving from sysadmin into DevOps.
Demonstrated ability to write idempotent, role-based, well-tested playbooks (rather than one giant task list) is a strong signal of production maturity in interviews.
Understanding the Terraform-then-Ansible enterprise pairing (Session 109 → this session) is a common systems-design interview topic for Platform Engineer roles.

misconceptions: “Ansible and Terraform do the same job.” They're complementary: Terraform provisions infrastructure resources, Ansible configures software on top of already-existing infrastructure — using one in place of the other, rather than together, usually means fighting the tool.

“If a playbook runs without errors, it's idempotent.” A playbook can run successfully every time while still reporting “changed” every time (e.g., an overly broad shell task) — true idempotency means the second run reports no changes.

“Agentless means no security surface.” Ansible's push model still requires SSH access and privilege escalation on every managed host — that access itself is a security surface that must be controlled and audited just as carefully as an agent would be.

“Inventory is a one-time setup.” Static inventory files silently go stale as servers are added/removed; dynamic inventory querying the cloud provider directly is the enterprise-standard way to keep it accurate.
anchors: “Terraform builds the house, Ansible furnishes it” — provisioning vs configuring, the core division of labor with IaC.
“Idempotent means boring on the second run” — a well-written playbook's second run should report all “ok,” zero “changed.”
“Roles are Ansible's modules” — reusable, parameterized, shareable, exactly like Terraform modules from Session 109.
“Always `--check` before you `apply`-equivalent” — dry-run new or risky playbooks before letting them touch production.

| v SSH connect (key-based auth) -> copy small Python module to /tmp | v Execute module on remote host -> compare current vs desired state | v Report: ok (no change) | changed (modified) | failed | v Notified handlers run once at end of play (e.g., restart service) End-to-End Provisioning + Configuration diagram: end-to-end handoff [ Terraform ] -> VM exists, network attached, security group open | [ Ansible ] -> packages installed, config templated, service running | [ Load Balancer / Reverse Proxy ] -> host added to healthy pool | [ Traffic served ]
